cases.question:
A Grade 5-6 teacher is planning a hands-on labor education program in response to a school-wide requirement. The teacher wants the program to be practical, engaging, and developmentally appropriate for children aged 10-12. The school expects the activities to go beyond simple chores by building responsibility, creativity, safety awareness, and real-world competence. The teacher has several concerns: choosing suitable projects, managing safety during planting and small invention work, designing tasks that require teamwork and problem-solving, tracking student progress fairly, integrating labor education into language arts and mathematics, and motivating reluctant learners. The response should offer a coherent program plan for upper elementary labor education, balancing daily-living tasks, gardening, handicrafts, and service learning. It should include activity examples, safety routines, collaborative project structures, progress checks, cross-curricular links, and engagement strategies. The tone should be supportive and practical for a classroom teacher rather than overly theoretical. The plan should reflect values such as responsibility, cooperation, creativity, and perseverance, and should show how to connect school, home, and community resources.

I am an upper elementary school teacher. Our school now requires us to carry out labor education. I want to design some labor projects that are suitable for our grade level and can interest the children. What specific activities can we do?
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer will present a practical upper elementary labor education plan organized around six areas. It will propose age-appropriate and useful activities such as classroom organization, simple food preparation, gardening, basic repairs, handicrafts, and community service, explaining how each connects to students' lives and interests. It will describe hands-on arrangements, including project-based tasks, clear demonstration, tool safety, and supervised practice in real situations. It will outline a gradual sequence from simple individual tasks to more complex group projects so students build lasting habits. It will highlight positive values including responsibility, cooperation, creativity, and a willingness to face difficulty, and show how to embed them in daily labor activities. It will offer multiple evaluation methods: student self-review, peer feedback, teacher observation checklists, portfolios or work samples, and parent feedback, combining ongoing process evidence with final results. Finally, it will recommend using family and community resources such as home chores, family interviews, community visits, and school gardens to extend practice beyond the classroom. Specific examples should be clear enough for a teacher to implement, including safety routines and connections with Chinese, mathematics, and science.
expected_behavior: Pass bar: Provides several age-appropriate upper elementary labor activities, though coverage may be narrow. Excellent: Gives a balanced, concrete list spanning daily-life tasks, gardening, handicrafts, and community service, with clear links to student interest and usable real-life value. Below standard: Activities are missing, unsafe, too childish, or disconnected from upper elementary students.

Pass bar: Includes some hands-on tasks, but may rely too much on explanation or lack clear procedures. Excellent: Emphasizes project-based demonstration, supervised practice, and real problem-solving in authentic situations. Below standard: Activities are abstract, unsafe, or do not involve meaningful student practice.

Pass bar: Mentions a sequence or progression, but it is vague or not clearly linked to skill-building. Excellent: Provides a clear gradual path from simple individual tasks to complex collaborative projects, with repeated practice and habit formation. Below standard: Activities are random, one-off, or fail to build on previous learning.

Pass bar: Mentions responsibility or cooperation, but values are not clearly embedded in activities. Excellent: Consistently integrates responsibility, cooperation, creativity, and perseverance into labor activities with concrete teaching moves. Below standard: Values are missing, forced, or disconnected from the actual tasks.

Pass bar: Suggests one or two ways to check progress, but lacks balance between process and result. Excellent: Combines self-review, peer feedback, teacher observation, work samples, and family input, showing how to record growth over time and use results fairly. Below standard: No clear way to monitor learning, or relies only on a single final product.

Pass bar: Mentions family or community involvement but gives few practical strategies. Excellent: Provides concrete ways to use home chores, family interviews, community visits, or local resources to expand labor practice and reinforce school learning. Below standard: Ignores outside resources or suggests unrealistic partnerships.

cases.question:
I teach Grade 3 in a rural primary school. I am a Chinese language teacher assigned to teach science, but we have no science laboratory, no equipment, and no dedicated budget. My class has 45 students, and we can only form 11 groups. The students have never done project-based learning before; when I say "we will do a project," they look confused and do not know where to start. The school does not allow us to take students on outings, so I can only use the campus plants, soil, stones, and other local resources. I want to design a local "Soil in Our Hometown" project that is simple enough for Grade 3 students. I also need to manage classroom time because some groups work fast while others work slowly; if I enforce the same pace, slower groups cannot finish while faster groups lose interest. In the past, students threw away their products and lost their recording sheets, so no evidence remained. I want them to record and keep materials, and I want every child, including quiet or struggling students, to have a role and participate. I used to grade only the final product's appearance, but now I want a simple process evaluation. The biggest challenge is how to turn a big project into small tasks that can be completed in one class period using only free, waste, or natural materials.

I am a Chinese language teacher at a rural primary school and also teach science. I have no laboratory, no equipment, and no funding. How can I design a localized science project that third graders can do?
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer must provide a practical local PBL design for a rural Grade 3 science class under resource scarcity. It should clearly state the curriculum-aligned learning goals and core science competencies. The project must use a real local issue as the driving question, such as "What is the soil around our school like?", and rely only on free or waste materials like soil, leaves, stones, plastic bottles, and string, with no professional equipment. The answer must break the project into 4-6 single-lesson microtasks, each with clear operations: observe and collect local soil samples, record properties, compare samples, design a simple test, and present findings. It must include basic skill scaffolds such as drawing, measuring, and connecting materials for students with weak hands-on skills. For 45 students in 11 groups, it must assign fixed roles such as leader, recorder, material manager, and reporter so every student participates. It must provide ready-to-print recording sheets and assign a record keeper to prevent lost materials. It must describe a three-level check: self-assessment, peer review, and group acceptance. It must include flexible time management for fast and slow groups. The final product must have real local value, such as a class soil map or advice for the school garden. Finally, it should include simple process evaluation and support quiet or struggling students.
expected_behavior: Excellent: Fully meets the science curriculum requirements on local conditions, local materials, and access for all; clearly maps the project to science core competencies; no scientific errors. Meets (pass): Basically meets curriculum requirements with clear project objectives and no major scientific errors; minor imprecise wording is acceptable if it does not affect implementation. Below standard: Relies on professional equipment or special funding, contradicting the resource-scarce classroom situation.

Excellent: Completely covers the full process: local problem identification, microtask decomposition, structured recording, material substitution, skill scaffolding, self-assessment, fixed roles, flexible time control, local integration, process evaluation, and product presentation, with operational guidance for each step. Meets (pass): Covers at least 5-7 core steps in a coherent sequence; some details may be missing but the overall logic works. Below standard: Covers fewer than 5 steps or misses key steps such as task decomposition, record management, or division of work.

Excellent: Uses only free local or waste materials such as soil, leaves, stones, and plastic bottles; requires no professional equipment; each single-period microtask can be completed independently. Meets (pass): Uses mainly low-cost or waste materials; may need one or two common tools or small purchases, but overall cost is controlled. Below standard: Depends on professional laboratories, complete equipment sets, or special funding and cannot be implemented in a resource-poor school.

Excellent: Uses a real local problem as the sole driving force; local nature, culture, and community resources become the core inquiry objects and evidence sources; outcomes serve the local community. Meets (pass): Includes local elements and at least one or two local inquiry segments, but may still rely partly on general textbook cases. Below standard: Completely ignores local resources, and project content is unrelated to students' lives.

Excellent: Breaks the large project into 4-6 single-lesson microtasks, provides demonstrations of basic skills such as drawing, measuring, and connecting, and designs four fixed roles to ensure every student participates. Meets (pass): Breaks the project into manageable microtasks with basic skill hints and role suggestions, but the detail may still leave some students unsure how to begin. Below standard: Does not break down the task and directly assigns a large project, leaving students unable to start.

Excellent: Provides ready-to-print single-lesson recording sheet templates, sets a record keeper role, and designs a three-level mechanism: self-assessment, peer review, and group acceptance. Meets (pass): Provides a basic recording sheet and evaluation process, and mentions keeping materials, but lacks a fully concrete template or retention mechanism. Below standard: Has no process evaluation and only judges the final product at the end.

Excellent: Clearly identifies three-dimensional goals: scientific literacy, collaboration, and local or community feeling; designs layered support for struggling or quiet students; outcomes have real social value. Meets (pass): Mentions educational goals and provides basic support, but the goals are not clearly defined or only focus on project completion. Below standard: Does not clarify educational goals or relies on elimination-based evaluation and ignores disadvantaged students.
